title: Stoic week
hookLine: modern Stoics run a week-long practice experiment

lines: A HANDBOOK, A MORNING, A NIGHT.
cards: A sign-up form, an online handbook, a short reading for each morning, a set of questions for each night.
Far from Athens, and long after it, a group of modern Stoic teachers and researchers runs a week of Stoic practice, open to anyone.
People from different jobs and countries do the same exercises on the same days, then report back how the week went. Part course, part experiment.
Back in year two, this path spent a long stretch with the Stoics, from a Stoic morning to a year on the porch. Today the porch opens again, as a test you run on yourself for one week.

teach.b: Tradition says the Stoics took their name from a painted porch in Athens, the Stoa, where Zeno taught in public. The porch was never a temple. People walked past, and some stopped to listen.
A Stoic week keeps that spirit: the practice happens at the desk and the dinner table, built on three old habits. First, the morning preview.
Marcus Aurelius wrote in his notebook, "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial." It sounds gloomy. It isn't.
He goes on to say none of them can harm his character, and that he was made to work alongside them.
The preview is a way of not being ambushed. Second, sorting through the day. Epictetus opens his handbook plainly: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not."
Your judgments and choices are in your power. The traffic, the weather and other people's moods are not.

teach.h: DAY: WHICH PILE IS THIS IN?
teach.b: All day, a Stoic week asks: which pile is this in?
Third, the evening review. Seneca describes ending each day by questioning himself, in paraphrase: what bad habit did I cure today, what fault did I resist, in what way am I better? Not a trial.
More like a coach replaying the tape.
Prepare, sort, review. It's small enough to try for seven days, and that's the point. A week turns the porch from something you read about into something you can check.

how: Modern Stoics run a week of practice open to the public, with a handbook, a morning reading and preview, exercises for sorting what is and isn't in one's power during the day, and an evening review; many people also keep these habits on their own.

games.q: you're stuck in traffic and already late. a Stoic week asks one question. which one?
o: which pile is this in: in my power or not?
how do I make the time up?
games.why: Epictetus opens his handbook with it. the traffic isn't in your power; your judgment about it is.

practice: Run the morning preview for whatever is left of today: who or what might test you? Name it plainly.
Then take one worry and sort it, the part in your power, your judgment and response, from the part that isn't, and let the second pile rest where it is.
